title: How to make a whodunnit from crosswords
gist: A novelist explains building his police procedural 'Phantom at the Feast' by using the solutions of 51 archived Guardian quick crosswords from the mid-1980s as an Oulipo-style 'lexical constraint', one crossword per chapter. The incidental commercial history is the sharper signal: the crossword's 1913 invention created enough latent demand that a 1924 gap in the market — no book of crossword puzzles existed — launched Simon & Schuster on an instant bestseller.

themes.theme: Crosswords as a business origin story

insights.claim: The modern crossword was born on 21st December 1913 when Liverpudlian journalist Arthur Wynne ran a 'Wordcross' puzzle in the New York World, and its commercial importance was only understood when an edition printed without the crossword drew many letters of complaint.
insights.speaker: Tony White
insights.so_what: The classic demonstration that a low-cost engagement feature can become the reason readers buy — the discovery mechanism was removal, not analytics.
insights.locator: While certain acrostic puzzles and palindromic word squares

insights.claim: In 1924 piano salesman Richard Simon, asked by an aunt for a book of crossword puzzles that did not exist, set up a company with Max Schuster, editor of a motor industry trade journal, to publish one — and that first book of crossword puzzles was an instant bestseller for Simon & Schuster.
insights.speaker: Tony White
insights.so_what: A major publishing house was founded on a single unmet-demand observation about a newspaper puzzle — a case study in adjacent-format monetisation of proven engagement.
insights.quote: That first ever book of crossword puzzles became an instant best seller for Simon & Schuster.
insights.locator: Apparently, one fan of Wynne’s puzzles

insights.claim: Puzzle attachment remains near-universal a century later: at book events, crosswords are consistently what audiences want to discuss, because almost everyone either is, knows, or is related to a 'crossword fiend'.
insights.speaker: Tony White
insights.so_what: Evidence of extraordinarily durable, cross-generational engagement with a simple text format — the demand characteristic that underpins puzzle subscriptions as a media revenue line.
insights.quote: Almost everyone either is, knows or is related to a “crossword fiend”.
insights.locator: At book events, audiences have been intrigued

themes.theme: Constraint as a creative production method

insights.claim: Oulipo — the 'Ouvroir de Littérature Potentielle' founded by François Le Lionnais and Raymond Queneau — proposed using arbitrary-seeming rules, or 'constraints', as the productive engine of literature, a method that produced Georges Perec's La Disparition, a novel written without the letter E.
insights.speaker: Tony White
insights.so_what: The constraint-first method is a transferable generative framework: imposed arbitrary rules force output away from default patterns — directly relevant to how generative systems are prompted and steered.

insights.claim: Italo Calvino wrote The Castle of Crossed Destinies by dealing Tarot cards into a grid and tracing imagery up, down, across and diagonally, describing the Tarot as a visual crossword — and the author inverted this, using crossword solutions as a lexical Tarot.
insights.speaker: Tony White
insights.so_what: A concrete recipe for turning any structured archive into a story generator — the same logic behind randomised-seed generative workflows.
insights.quote: might these old Guardian crosswords comprise what Oulipo would call a “lexical constraint”?
insights.locator: In the blinding flash of inspiration

insights.claim: The author wrote each chapter of Phantom at the Feast using all of the solutions from a particular Guardian quick crossword, and all 51 completed crosswords used were exhibited at Matt's Gallery, London, as part of a display about the novel's development.
insights.speaker: Tony White
insights.so_what: The visible process artefacts became an exhibitable asset in their own right — a template for extending a single book's commercial and cultural surface area.
insights.locator: That’s why we recently exhibited all 51

insights.claim: Following a lexical constraint scrupulously drives plot in directions the writer did not choose — when words like 'erect' and 'flagrante' appear in an upcoming source crossword, romance becomes structurally unavoidable and the author must work out who falls for whom.
insights.speaker: Tony White
insights.so_what: Constraint-driven generation surrenders authorial control in exchange for novelty — the same trade-off that governs the value and the risk of stochastic creative tools.
insights.locator: Following the constraint scrupulously can take a story

insights.claim: Georges Perec, the Oulipian lipogram novelist, spent the last years of his life as crossword setter for Le Point magazine, and 2026 marks the 50th anniversary of Raymond Queneau's death.
insights.speaker: Tony White
insights.so_what: Anniversary years reliably generate reissue, exhibition and adaptation activity around a literary estate — a scheduling signal for cultural programming.

insights.claim: Historical crossword solutions function like a time capsule or cultural core sample, capturing the preoccupations and personalities of their moment, which makes back-page marginalia a richer seam of period authenticity than front-page news coverage.
insights.speaker: Tony White
insights.so_what: Overlooked, high-frequency, low-status archive material carries dense signal about the period that produced it — a reusable research heuristic for any historical dataset.
insights.quote: Like a time capsule—a cultural core sample from deep in the frozen continent of the past—the crosswords seem to capture the preoccupations and personalities of the time.
insights.locator: I discovered that those historical crossword solutions

insights.claim: Crosswords record the subtle evolution of written language, including archaic hyphenations that have since disappeared such as 'tea-shop', alongside larger cultural shifts — when Jacques Chirac appears in a 1985 Guardian crossword it is as a former mayor of Paris, not a future president of France.
insights.speaker: Tony White
insights.so_what: Dated, high-frequency puzzle corpora are a precisely timestamped record of usage and public salience — a genuinely usable proxy dataset for tracking attention drift over decades.
insights.quote: When Jacques Chirac appears in a Guardian crossword from 1985, it’s as a former mayor of Paris, not the future president of France.
insights.locator: Crosswords also capture the subtle evolution

insights.claim: The word 'rebus' appeared as the solution to 'Pictorial pun (5)' in the Guardian quick crossword of 29th May 1985, just weeks after Scottish postgraduate Ian Rankin began writing his first Inspector John Rebus novel in March 1985 — and reusing that clue today the fictional character trumps the original dictionary definition.
insights.speaker: Tony White
insights.so_what: A clean illustration of intellectual property overwriting general language — once a franchise dominates a word, its commercial meaning displaces the dictionary one.
insights.locator: When the word “rebus” appeared as the solution

themes.theme: The 1984-85 policing playbook as subject matter

insights.claim: The novel's investigation reaches back to the Miners' Strike and the Battle of Orgreave on 18th June 1984, and to the death during the strike of a union official at a fictional riot in Sheffield city centre.
insights.speaker: Tony White
insights.so_what: Mid-1980s British social conflict remains live commercial subject matter in crime fiction — a durable market for period political material.
insights.locator: When the key witness in a trafficking investigation

insights.claim: The aggressive public-order policing playbook honed against pickets at the Orgreave coking plant was seemingly applied with extreme violence on 1st June 1985 against a convoy of hippies travelling to the Stonehenge Free Festival, in what became known as the Battle of the Beanfield and remains one of the largest civilian mass arrests in British history.
insights.speaker: Tony White
insights.so_what: Tactics developed against one target group get redeployed against unrelated others — a pattern worth watching wherever new policing or surveillance capability is first justified by a narrow use case.
insights.quote: remains one of the largest civilian mass arrests in British history
insights.locator: On that day, a “playbook” of aggressive public-order policing

insights.claim: Phantom at the Feast (No Exit Press, £12.99) is the follow-up to The Fountain in the Forest (2018) and continues the story of Metropolitan police Detective Sergeant Rex King of Holborn Police Station, whose reversible name is itself both crossword clue and solution.
insights.speaker: Tony White
insights.so_what: An independent publisher sustaining a formally experimental crime series across eight years indicates a viable niche between literary and genre markets.
insights.locator: My latest detective novel, the police procedural whodunnit
